{{Short description|Fallacious argument exploiting connection to nationalism}}
'''Flag-waving''' is a [[fallacious argument]] or [[propaganda technique]] used to justify an action based on the undue connection to nationalism or patriotism or benefit for an idea, group or country.<ref name="TabernerCheng1993">{{cite book|author1=Ferrán Valls i Taberner|author2=Chia-Jui Cheng|title=Ciencia política comparada y derecho y economía en las relaciones internacionales: estudios en homenaje a Ferran Valls i Taberner|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=djuFAAAAMAAJ|access-date=10 August 2013|year=1993|publisher=Cátedra de Historia del Derecho y de las Instituciones, Facultad de Derecho, Universidad de Málaga|page=7219|isbn=9788460460589 |quote=Today, indeed, flag-waving has become a quite common generic term denoting the deliberate appeal to nationalistic emotions and prejudices.}}</ref><ref name="Hein2011">{{cite book|author=Nicole Hein|title=Spinning Coverage: An Analysis of The New York Times' Reporting on the War in Iraq in Light of the U.S. Administration's Spin and Propaganda Efforts|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=XuAwGd4PH5oC&pg=PA33|access-date=9 August 2013|date=7 November 2011|publisher=GRIN Verlag|isbn=978-3-656-04831-2|page=33|quote=Flag-waving is a popular propaganda technique, meaning that an action is justified "on the grounds that doing [what is promoted, in this case support the war] will make one more patriotic, or in some way benefit a group, country, or idea.}}</ref> It is a variant of [[argumentum ad populum]].<ref name="Cohen2004">{{cite book|author=Daniel Harry Cohen|title=Arguments and Metaphors in Philosophy|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=5bMb4ckHwq4C&pg=PA59|access-date=9 August 2013|date=1 January 2004|publisher=University Press of America|isbn=978-0-7618-2677-4|page=59|quote= ...ad Hominen ridicule, ad Misehcordiam tears, or ad Populum flag-waving - all logical fallacies...}}</ref> This fallacy [[Appeal to emotion|appeals to emotion]] instead to logic of the audience aiming to [[psychological manipulation|manipulate]] them to win an argument. All ad populum fallacies are based on the presumption that the recipients already have certain beliefs, biases, and prejudices about the issue.<ref name="Bell1990">{{cite book|author=Kathleen Bell|title=Developing arguments: strategies for reaching audiences|url=https://archive.org/details/developingargume0000bell|url-access=registration|access-date=9 August 2013|date=February 1990|publisher=Wadsworth Pub. Co.|page=[https://archive.org/details/developingargume0000bell/page/284 284]|isbn=9780534121921 |quote=The ad populum argument presumes that the audience already holds a particular attitude and specific beliefs on the issue.}}</ref>

If flag-waving is based on connecting to some [[symbol]] of patriotism or nationalism it is a form of appeal to stirring symbols which can be based on undue connection not only to nationalism but also to some religious or cultural symbols—for example, a politician appearing on TV with children, farmer, teacher, together with the "common" man, etc.

The act of flag-waving is a superficial display of support or loyalty to, for example, a [[nation]] or a [[political party]].<ref name="Chambers1998">{{cite book|author=Allied Chambers|title=The Chambers Dictionary|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=pz2ORay2HWoC&pg=RA1-PA609|access-date=14 August 2013|year=1998|publisher=Allied Publishers|isbn=978-81-86062-25-8|page=609}}</ref>
